DAT 301 Project 2¶

What Team Efficiency Metrics Best Predict Winning in the NBA (Extended)?¶

Rishit Maiti

04/30/2026

Introduction¶

Sports analytics has become an essential tool in understanding performance and success in many sports including professional basketball, baseball, and many more. While traditional statistics such as points, assists, and shooting percentages have long been used to evaluate teams’ performance and provide useful insights, they do not fully cover the efficiency and overall impact of a team’s performance. Modern analytics introduce efficiency-based metrics that provide deeper insights.

In recent years, advanced metrics such as offensive rating, defensive rating, and turnover percentage have been used more frequently. These metrics provide a deeper understanding of how efficiently teams score points and defend.

The goal/purpose of this project is to analyze and determine which team-level performance and efficiency metrics best predict winning in the NBA. Specifically, my analysis will investigate and go over how efficiency metrics and variables such as offensive rating, defensive rating, shooting efficiency, and turnovers influence team success of the number of games a team wins.

This project is based on the same NBA topic as my Project 1, but this time around, it is fully done in Python and includes additional visualizations and a broader analysis.

Background and Problem Definition¶

In my Project 1, I studied how NBA team-level efficiency metrics relate to wins. I found that offensive rating, defensive rating, and net rating were among the strongest predictors of team success, and the simplified regression model explained about 88.7% of the variation in wins.

For Project 2, I am converting that R-based analysis into Python and also upgrading it. In addition to recreating the major steps from Project 1, I will include more polished visualizations, a heatmap, a pairplot, a top-10 net rating chart, and an era comparison to deepen the analysis.

Main Research Question¶

What team efficiency metrics best predict winning in the NBA?

Goals of my Project¶

  • Clean and prepare NBA team data in Python
  • Perform exploratory data analysis using pandas
  • Create visualizations with matplotlib and seaborn
  • Analyze correlations between key variables
  • Build regression models in Python
  • Compare modern NBA eras to extend the original analysis

Dataset and Source¶

The dataset used in this project comes from the same NBA statistics source used in Project 1. The entire dataset comes from a Kaggle NBA statistics dataset, which contains team-by-team level statistics across multiple NBA seasons.

Key/Main variables used¶

  • w = Number of wins
  • l = Number of losses
  • WinPct = Win Percentage
  • mov = Margin of Victory
  • o_rtg = Offensive rating (points scored per 100 possessions)
  • d_rtg = Defensive rating (points allowed per 100 possessions),
  • n_rtg = Net rating (offensive rating - defensive rating)
  • pace = Game pace / number of possessions per game
  • ts_percent = True shooting percentage
  • e_fg_percent = Effective field goal percentage
  • tov_percent = Turnover percentage

This dataset is good for this analysis as it provides both traditional and advanced performance metrics, which will allow us to evaluate which factors most strongly influence team success.

Data Cleaning and Preparation¶

In Project 1, I filtered the data to include only seasons from 2000 onward, created a win percentage variable, selected the main variables for analysis, and removed missing values. I follow the same overall process here in Python.

We start by filtering/loading and organizing/cleaning the dataset. Our main goal is to focus on and include only modern NBA seasons (2000s to present-day), create a variable for win percentage, and ensure that the dataset is usable for further analysis.

In [121]:
df2 = df[df["season"] >= 2000].copy()

df2["WinPct"] = df2["w"] / (df2["w"] + df2["l"])

vars_keep = [
    "season", "team", "w", "l", "WinPct",
    "mov", "o_rtg", "d_rtg", "n_rtg", "pace",
    "ts_percent", "e_fg_percent", "tov_percent"
]

# Check all missing values
nba_raw = df2[vars_keep].copy()
nba_raw.isnull().sum()

# Remove all missing values
nba = nba_raw.dropna().copy()
nba.isnull().sum()

nba = df2[vars_keep].dropna().copy()

# Import data from 1999-2000 NBA Season to most recent complete season (2024-2025) 
# I did not include most recent season (2025-2026) since it is still ongoing 
nba[(nba["season"] >= 2000) & (nba["season"] <= 2026)]

Data Cleaning Notes¶

  • I filtered/organized the data to include only seasons from 2000 onward in order to focus on modern NBA basketball and NBA play styles.
  • I created a new variable called WinPct to standardize team success and performance, and make it consistent across those seasons.
  • I selected only the variables most relevant to the analysis to simplify everything in my analysis.
  • I removed missing values to make sure the dataset is clean for modeling and visualization, as well as ensuring sconsistent results.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) — Histograms¶

EDA is used to understand the distribution and relationships of variables before building models.

In [123]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize = (12, 8))

axes[0, 0].hist(nba["w"], bins = 20, edgecolor = "black")
axes[0, 0].set_title("Histogram of Wins")
axes[0, 0].set_xlabel("Wins")
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("Frequency")

axes[0, 1].hist(nba["WinPct"], bins = 20, edgecolor = "black")
axes[0, 1].set_title("Histogram of Win Percentage")
axes[0, 1].set_xlabel("WinPct")
axes[0, 1].set_ylabel("Frequency")

axes[1, 0].hist(nba["mov"], bins = 20, edgecolor = "black")
axes[1, 0].set_title("Histogram of Margin of Victory")
axes[1, 0].set_xlabel("MOV")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("Frequency")

axes[1, 1].hist(nba["o_rtg"], bins = 20, edgecolor = "black")
axes[1, 1].set_title("Histogram of Offensive Rating")
axes[1, 1].set_xlabel("Offensive Rating")
axes[1, 1].set_ylabel("Frequency")

# Improve the looks
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Histogram Interpretations¶

Histogram of Wins: The distribution of wins appears approximately normal as it is centered around 40–45 wins. This reflects and aligns with the balanced nature of the NBA, where most teams hang around average performance, with fewer teams achieving very high or very low win totals.

Histogram of Win Percentage: Win percentage is also approximately normally distributed, with most teams falling between the range of 0.4 and 0.6. This indicates that the majority of teams perform near average, with relatively few extreme high-performing or low-performing teams.

Histogram of Margin of Victory: Margin of victory is centered around zero and shows a roughly symmetric distribution. This suggests that most teams are either slightly outscored or are slightly outscored by opponents, with only a few teams having very large positive or negative margins.

Histogram of Offensive Rating: These histograms show that key variables like wins and win percentage are approximately normally distributed, with most teams clustered around average performance. Margin of victory is centered near zero, indicating that most teams are relatively balanced overall. Offensive rating also shows a fairly normal distribution, suggesting that most teams fall within a similar efficiency range, with only a few extreme outliers. Basically, wins and win percentage appear relatively normally distributed, while margin of victory and offensive rating show moderate-to-no variation across teams.

Overall, in general, the distributions of wins and win percentage appear roughly centered around average team performance, which is consistent with what I found in Project 1. Margin of victory is centered near zero, and offensive rating is spread across a fairly normal range. These plots suggest that most teams cluster around average performance, while relatively few teams are extreme outliers.

Scatterplots and Relationships with Wins¶

In [124]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize = (12, 10))

sns.regplot(data = nba, x = "mov", y = "w", ax = axes[0, 0], scatter_kws = {"alpha": 0.5})
axes[0, 0].set_title("Wins vs Margin of Victory")

sns.regplot(data = nba, x = "o_rtg", y = "w", ax = axes[0, 1], scatter_kws = {"alpha": 0.5})
axes[0, 1].set_title("Wins vs Offensive Rating")

sns.regplot(data = nba, x = "d_rtg", y="w", ax = axes[1, 0], scatter_kws = {"alpha": 0.5})
axes[1, 0].set_title("Wins vs Defensive Rating")

sns.regplot(data = nba, x = "tov_percent", y = "w", ax = axes[1, 1], scatter_kws = {"alpha": 0.5})
axes[1, 1].set_title("Wins vs Turnover Percentage")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Scatterplot Interpretation¶

Wins vs Margin of Victory:¶

There is a very strong positive linear relationship between margin of victory and wins. Teams with higher average scoring margins tend to win significantly more games, making this one of the strongest predictors of success.

Wins vs Offensive Rating¶

There is a clear positive relationship between offensive rating and wins. Teams that score more efficiently tend to win more games, although the relationship is slightly more spread out compared to margin of victory.

Wins vs Defensive Rating¶

There is a strong negative relationship between defensive rating and wins. Since lower defensive rating indicates better defense, this shows that teams that allow fewer points per possession tend to win more games.

Wins vs Turnover Percentage¶

The relationship between turnover percentage and wins appears weaker and slightly negative. Teams that commit fewer turnovers tend to win more games, but this effect is less pronounced compared to offensive and defensive efficiency metrics.

These plots support the patterns I found in Project 1. Margin of victory and net rating show very strong positive relationships with wins. Specifically, Margin of victory shows a very strong positive linear relationship with wins, showing that teams that con- sistently outscore their opponents tend to win more games, which is expected.

Both offensive and defensive ratings show strong linear relationships with wins, while turnover percentages show a weaker/negative trend. Offensive rating also shows a positive relationship with wins, while defensive rating shows a strong negative relationship, meaning better defenses (lower values) are associated with more wins.

Turnover percentage appears to have a weaker negative relationship with wins. Overall, efficiency metrics appear to matter a great deal in predicting team success. Overall, these scatter plots help us visualize clear relationships between variables (efficiency metrics) and wins, particularly for offensive and defensive ratings. Overall, these scatter plots help us visualize clear relationships between variables (efficiency metrics) and wins, particularly for offensive and defensive ratings.

Additional Visualization: Net Rating vs Wins:¶

To further prove my point, I will include a visualization that will analyze the relationship between net rating (n_rtg) and wins. Net rating combines both offensive and defensive performance into a single metric, making ssit a strong indicator of overall team strength.

In [125]:
plt.figure(figsize = (8, 6))
sns.regplot(data = nba, x = "n_rtg", y = "w", scatter_kws = {"alpha": 0.5})
plt.title("Wins vs Net Rating")
plt.xlabel("Net Rating")
plt.ylabel("Wins")
plt.show()

Wins vs Net Rating:¶

This plot shows a very strong positive relationship between net rating and wins. Teams with higher net ratings consistently win more games, which reinforces the idea that overall efficiency (offense + defense combined) is one of the best predictors of team success.

Correlation Analysis¶

The correlation matrix confirms that the relationships observed in the scatter plots are accurate. Wins are strongly and positively correlated with margin of victory, net rating, and offensive rating, and negatively correlated with defensive rating. Net rating shows an extremely high correlation with wins, indicating that it is one of the strongest overall predictors of team success. Turnover percentage and pace also show weaker correlations, suggesting they have less direct impact on wins compared to efficiency metrics.

Pace and turnover percentage have weaker relationships with wins compared to the major efficiency metrics. Basically, strong correlations are shown between wins and efficiency metrics such as offensive rating, defensive rating, and net rating. This matches the core findings from Project 1.

Net Rating Upgrade Interpretation¶

This plot adds another layer to the project by highlighting the teams with the strongest overall combined offensive and defensive efficiency. Since net rating was one of the strongest predictors of wins in Project 1, I decided to figure out the top-5 performing teams based on net rating, which is the difference between a team's offensive and defensive rating. In simple terms, this is stat is by how much a team outscores their opponents.

Full Model Notes¶

This full regression model includes all selected variables to evaluate their combined effect on team wins. In Project 1, the full model showed issues related to multicollinearity because net rating overlaps strongly with offensive and defensive rating. I expected a similar issue here in Python as well. This model helps identify which efficiency metrics are significant predictors before we begin simplifying the model to help us better understand and interpret the results accurately.

Simplified Model Interpretation¶

This simplified model is easier to interpret while still making it an effective tool to use when making predictions. Regression models are used to determine how multiple variables can simultaneously affect wins. This simplified model makes it easier for us to interpret the data while still being able to make effective predictions. In Project 1, the simplified model explained about 88.7% of the variation in wins and showed that offensive rating and defensive rating were especially important. This Python version is intended to reproduce and confirm those main findings.

Regression Findings Summary¶

Based on the simplified model:

  • Offensive rating should have a strong positive relationship with wins.
  • Defensive rating should have a strong negative relationship with wins.
  • Margin of victory is usually significant, although its coefficient may be affected by overlap with related metrics.
  • Effective field goal percentage may become less significant once offensive rating is included.
  • Turnover percentage may still matter, but usually less strongly than offensive and defensive rating.

This aligns well with my Project 1 results, where offensive rating and defensive rating were the strongest predictors and the model had a very strong fit.

Residual Analysis¶

In [133]:
plt.figure(figsize = (8, 6))
plt.scatter(model2.fittedvalues, model2.resid, alpha = 0.5)
plt.axhline(0, color = "red", linestyle = "--")
plt.title("Residual Plot")
plt.xlabel("Fitted Wins")
plt.ylabel("Residuals")
plt.show()

Residual Plot Analysis¶

The residual plot shows that residuals are randomly scattered around zero with no clear pattern, indicating that the linear model assumptions are pretty much satisfied. The spread of residuals appears relatively consistent across fitted values, suggesting no strong and unequal variability. Overall, this indicates that the model provides a good fit for predicting wins.

In [134]:
plt.figure(figsize = (8, 6))
plt.hist(model2.resid, bins = 20, edgecolor = "black")
plt.title("Histogram of Residuals")
plt.xlabel("Residuals")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.show()

Residual Analysis Interpretation¶

The residual plot helps check whether the residuals are scattered randomly around zero, while the histogram helps evaluate whether the residuals are approximately normally distributed. Residual plots are used to evaluate model assumptions. Specifically, we analyze the linear model, constant variance, and normality of errors. In Project 1, the residuals appeared reasonably well-behaved, supporting the idea that the linear model was appropriate. This Python version checks the same assumptions again. Now, in Project 2, the residuals appear to be randomly distributed, which shows that the model is appropriate. This supports the assumption of normally distributed errors in the regression model.

The comparison between eras shows how the relationship between team efficiency and winning is different between the earlier seasons in the 2000s and the modern NBA seasons in the 2020s, specifically the most recent pace-and-space era dominated by three-point shooting. By separating the data into two periods, I can see whether offensive performance has become even more important in the modern NBA.

Residual plots are used to evaluate model assumptions. Specifically, we analyze the linear model, constant variance, and normality of errors. In Project 1, the residuals appeared reasonably well-behaved, supporting the idea that the linear model was appropriate. This Python version checks the same assumptions again. Now, in Project 2, the residuals appear to be randomly distributed, which shows that the model is appropriate. This supports the assumption of normally distributed errors in the regression model.

Results and Interpretation¶

The simplified regression model explains approximately 88.7% of the variability in team wins (R² = 0.8873), indicating a strong fit and that the selected variables are highly predictive of team success.

Overall Model Strength: My model explains that approximately 88.7% of the variability in team wins, which indicates a very strong relationship between the selected efficiency metrics and overall team success. This suggests that the variables I used in this model can be highly effective when it comes to predicting wins in the NBA.

Key Findings:¶

  • Offensive Rating (o_rtg)

    • Offensive rating has a strong positive and statistically significant relationship with wins, indicating that teams with better offensive efficiency tend to win more games.
    • Coefficient: +3.69
    • p-value: 1.09e-07 (very significant)

  • Defensive Rating (d_rtg)

    • Defensive rating has a strong negative and statistically significant relationship with wins.
    • Lower defensive ratings are better, which suggests that strong defense is crucial for success.

  • Margin of Victory (mov)

    • Margin of victory is statistically significant, but its negative coefficient may be affected due to multicollinearity with other variables like offensive and defensive rating.
    • Coefficient: -1.57
    • p-value: 0.028

  • Effective Field Goal Percentage (e_fg_percent)

    • This variable is not statistically significant when other variables are included, meaning that its effect may already be captured due to the offensive rating.
    • p-value: 0.46

  • Turnover Percentage (tov_percent)

    • Turnover percentage shows a marginally significant negative relationship with wins, which shows that limiting turnovers may contribute to team success, even though its effects are weaker compared to the other variables.
    • p-value: 0.054

Overall, in general, these team efficiency metrics, especially offensive and defensive ratings, are the most significant when determining team success, while individual/traditional statistics may have a smaller impact when the efficiency is already accounted for. All of these show that overall team efficiency is more important than individual/traditional statistics.

Final Conclusion and Future Findings¶

My Python analysis basically had the same key results from my Project 1, which is that team efficiency metrics are very strong predictors of success in the NBA. Statistics like offensive rating, defensive rating, margin of victory, and net rating all show a very strong relationships with wins. Turnover percentage has a weak negative relationship. Also, pace appears to have less prediction power.

The regression results support the conclusion that overall team efficiency is more important than traditional counting statistics alone. This matches the main takeaway from Project 1, where the simplified model explained about 88.7% of the variation in team wins.

My Python Analysis is broader that Project 1 because it adds:

  • Correlation Heatmap
  • Pairplot
  • Top-10 Net Rating Visualization,
  • Era-by-era Comparison.

This analysis demonstrates that team efficiency metrics, particularly offensive and defensive ratings, are the strongest predictors of winning in the NBA. While traditional statistics such as shooting efficiency and turnovers contribute to performance, their impact is less significant when accounting for overall team efficiency. These findings highlight the importance of advanced metrics in modern basketball analysis, which can help us evaluate basketball success and provide valuable insights into the factors that drive team success and winning outcomes in the NBA.

Future Work: Future research could explore how these relationships change over time or differ across different eras of basketball and the NBA.

Overall, this project 2 shows how we can use Python tools like pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, and other similar things to find predictions and trends in the field of sports analytics.

Presentation Summary¶

In summary, the model explains about 89% (88.7 %) of the variation in wins, which shows a very strong relationship between team performance metrics and success. The most important factors identified were offensive rating and defensive rating, meaning that teams that score efficiently and defend well tend to win more games by a significant amount. Other variables like shooting efficiency and turnovers still play a big role, but their impact becomes less significant once overall team efficiency is taken into account.
